title: Breaking the 1.58-bit Barrier for Ternary LLMs
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 14 Sep 2026]
    Title:Breaking the 1.58-bit Barrier for Ternary LLMs
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Ternary Large Language Models (LLM) store every weight as one of three symbols $\{-1,0,+1\}$, so the cost of a ternary model is conventionally referenced to the information-theoretic $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ bits per weight. The prevailing deployment format packs five ternary weights into one byte (five-trit packing), and due to the power-of-two group sizes used in practice this rounds up to $1.625$ bits per weight. This effective storage bit-width treats the three symbols $\{-1,0,+1\}$ as equiprobable. We measure the actual symbol distribution of 29 ternary LLM models and find that zeros account for up to $51.5\%$ of all weights. Motivated by this finding, we introduce BITCOS, a simple distribution-adaptive layout comprised of a dense presence bitmap plus a compacted sign vector, and costs $2 - z$ bits per weight element given a zero density $z$ in the model's weights. BITCOS stores weights more compactly than the five-trit packing in 26 of the 29 tested models, and reaches $1.485$ bits per weight on the sparsest of them. BITCOS is amenable to efficient unpacking on modern processors and GPUs, and we present optimized unpacking sequences for AVX-512, AVX2 and Intel Xe2 GPUs. Measured against production state-of-the-art ternary matrix-vector multiplication kernels, at the zero densities real-world ternary models exhibit, the realized gain with our proposed layout is up to $1.28\times$. Finally, we illustrate end-to-end LLM inference results on 5 different platforms (client and server CPUs, integrated and discrete Xe2 GPUs) where decode throughput improves by up to $1.18\times$ on CPUs and $1.27\times$ on GPUs.

report.summary: New BITCOS layout exploits zero-heavy ternary LLM weights to store them below 1.58 bits, speeding CPU and GPU inference.
report.background: Ternary LLMs store each weight as -1, 0, or +1, giving an information-theoretic cost of log2(3) ≈ 1.585 bits per weight. In practice, deployment formats pack five ternary weights into one byte, rounding up to 1.625 bits and implicitly treating the three symbols as equally likely. This assumption has shaped ternary kernels, memory layouts, and hardware expectations, especially around BitNet-style models. But real ternary models are not perfectly balanced: quantization and training often leave many weights exactly zero. The paper measures 29 ternary LLM models and finds zero densities up to 51.5%, motivating a distribution-adaptive storage format that exploits this sparsity rather than ignoring it.
key_points: The paper measures actual symbol distributions in 29 ternary LLMs and finds zeros can make up 51.5% of all weights, contradicting the common assumption that -1, 0, and +1 are equiprobable.
BITCOS uses a dense presence bitmap plus a compacted sign vector. Its storage cost is 2 - z bits per weight, where z is the model's zero density, adapting automatically to sparsity.
BITCOS beats conventional five-trit packing in 26 of 29 tested models and reaches 1.485 bits per weight on the sparsest model, below the usual 1.625-bit deployment format.
The authors provide optimized unpacking sequences for AVX-512, AVX2, and Intel Xe2 GPUs. Against state-of-the-art ternary matrix-vector kernels, realized gains reach up to 1.28x.
End-to-end inference tests across five client and server platforms show decode throughput improving by up to 1.18x on CPUs and 1.27x on GPUs.
The method targets memory-bandwidth-bound ternary inference, so benefits depend on real zero density and kernel integration rather than only on theoretical bit-width.
report.impact: For the AI industry, BITCOS shows that ternary LLM efficiency is not fixed at 1.58 or 1.625 bits; model statistics can be exploited for real memory and bandwidth savings. That matters for edge devices, client CPUs, and cost-sensitive server inference, where decode throughput and memory footprint are key. For developers, it suggests quantization pipelines and runtimes should track zero density and adopt adaptive layouts, bitmap unpacking, and SIMD/GPU kernels. Regular users could eventually see faster local models and lower memory use, especially for BitNet-style deployments. The main caveat is that gains require sparse ternary weights and software support, so broad impact depends on integration into popular inference stacks.
report.tools: Watch for a BITCOS reference implementation from the authors, plus ternary inference projects such as Microsoft's BitNet and bitnet.cpp, llama.cpp, and T-MAC. Intel oneDNN and Xe2 GPU kernel libraries may add bitmap unpacking paths. Hugging Face Optimum and Transformers quantization tooling could expose zero-density-aware layouts for evaluation.
